idiom_name: empty interface used in generic constraints and type sets
implementation_notes: C# permits empty interfaces and the compiler enforces conformance, so a marker interface remains the right tool when the category must appear in a generic constraint or a compile-time type set - Microsoft's CA1040 rule explicitly allows suppressing the warning for that case. At run time obj is IMarker is a cheap interface test, and the mark is inherited by every derived class. Use it when substitutability matters (a method may accept only marked arguments); use an attribute when you are merely recording a fact.
pitfalls: An empty interface cannot be unimplemented by a derived class, so the mark propagates to all subclasses whether or not they honour it.
CA1040 flags externally visible empty interfaces; suppress it only with the documented compile-time-type-set rationale.
Markers cannot annotate fields, methods or parameters and cannot carry values - that is attribute territory.

variants.name: Custom attribute for metadata
variants.idiom_name: custom Attribute class read with reflection
variants.implementation_notes: The .NET idiom for type facts is a custom attribute: [Serializable], [Flags] and user-defined attributes record metadata that code reads with reflection (IsDefined / GetCustomAttribute); attributes can carry values and target classes, fields, methods and parameters. They are not types, so they cannot appear in generic constraints - the trade that keeps marker interfaces alive. Prefer attributes for descriptive metadata and reserve marker interfaces for compile-time substitutability.
pitfalls: Reflection-based checks fail at run time, not compile time, and are slower than an interface test unless cached.
Attribute inheritance is opt-in via [Inherited] and works differently from interface implementation on interfaces and overridden members.
[Serializable] is a CLI flag while ISerializable is a contract with methods - do not treat them as interchangeable marker and behaviour.
